t: Count Distinct Integers After Removing Zeros
o: For each x in [1, n] we write x with all zero digits deleted (e.g., 10 becomes 1, 105 becomes 15). We must count distinct written values for n up to 1e15, so iterating is impossible. Key observation: stripping zeros from x yields a positive integer m with no zero digits, and m ≤ x ≤ n. Conversely every zero-free m ≤ n is produced (by x = m itself). Hence the answer is exactly the count of integers in [1, n] containing no digit 0 — a classic digit-DP / combinatorial count.
k: Stripped values are precisely the zero-free integers ≤ n.
Count them with digit DP: at each position choose digits 1..limit; free positions contribute a factor of 9.

a.i: For intuition: strip zeros from every x ≤ n and insert into a set. This is O(n · digits) and only works for tiny n, but validates the reduction.
s: For each x from 1 to n, remove '0' characters and parse.
a.t: O(n log n) — iterates all values up to n

a.i: Count zero-free integers ≤ n digit by digit. Walk the digits of n tightly; at position i, choosing any digit d in [1, s[i]-1] frees the remaining L-1-i positions, each with 9 choices, contributing 9^(L-1-i) per choice. If some digit of n is 0 the tight branch dies; if all digits are nonzero, n itself counts. Finally add all shorter zero-free numbers, Σ 9^len for len = 1..L-1.
s: Add Σ_{len=1}^{L-1} 9^len for numbers with fewer digits than n.
Scan digits of n left to right; at position i add (s[i]-1) * 9^(L-1-i) choices for digits 1..s[i]-1 (skip if s[i] = 0, then stop).
If the scan completes without hitting a 0, add 1 for n itself.
a.t: O(L^2) or O(L) with precomputed powers — L ≤ 16 digits

w: Prove the reduction carefully in an interview: stripping zeros never creates a zero-free number larger than x, and every zero-free m ≤ n maps to itself. Pitfalls: forgetting shorter-length numbers (the Σ 9^len term) and forgetting to count n itself when it is zero-free. Follow-up: count distinct stripped values in a range [l, r], or strip a different digit.
